A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S8377A

TITLE OF BILL:
An act
to amend the multiple dwelling law, in relation to
interim multiple dwellings in a city with a
population of one million or more persons; and
to amend chapter 405 of the laws of 1999, amending the real property tax
law relating to improving the administration of the school tax relief
(STAR) program, in relation to the effectiveness thereof and to amend
the tax law, in relation to video lottery gaming

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF THE BILL:
This bill will serve as a chapter amendment to bill numbers S.7178-A
and A.5667-C.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:
This bill would amend the definition of interim multiple dwelling to
only include a building where three or more families have lived
independently of each other for 12 consecutive months or longer
between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2009.

The bill would also establish other safety criteria that would have to
be met for a unit to be eligible as a loft protected by the loft law.
No unit could be located in a basement or cellar; each unit must have
at least one entrance that does not require passage through another
residential unit to reach the unit; each unit must have at least one
window opening onto a street, yard, or court; and each unit must be
at least 550 square feet in area.

Covered buildings cannot be located in an industrial business zone,
except lofts in the North Brooklyn and Williamsburg/Greenpoint
industrial business Zones and building located in that portion of the
Long Island city industrial business zone that is located north of
forty-fourth drive, south of Queens plaza north, and west of
twenty-third street may be included in the term "interim multiple
dwelling". Covered buildings will also include an area with
boundaries that encompass three blocks in Manhattan, including the
buildings located on the north side of West 24th Street, the south
side of West 27th Street, the east side of 11th Ave. and the west
side of 10th Ave. and that were occupied for residential purposes as
the residence or home of any two or more families living
independently from one another for a period of twelve consecutive
months during the period commencing January 1, 2008 and ending
December 31, 2009.

The loft board must determine in rules and regulations whether each
use set forth in groups 15 through 18, as defined in the
municipalities zoning law, constitutes a use inherently incompatible
with residential use. No change in

the use of the building would remove the protections of loft law from
the units that have been covered.

The bill would increase the maximum penalty that could be issued for a
violation of the loft board's rules or regulations from $1,000 to
$17,500.

The bill would allow the loft board to designate the environmental
control board as the enforcing entity for various provisions of its
rules and regulations. The environmental control board could issue
penalties up to $17,500 for violations and could issue judgments that
could be docketed and enforced. The department of buildings would be
able to issue any violations that the environmental control board
issues.

The bill would require that all applications for inclusion under loft
law be filed within six months after the loft board has finished
adopting as the rules and regulations necessary to implement the bill.

JUSTIFICATION:
This chapter amendment was drafted to address concerns that the
underlying legislation would allow lofts with insurmountable safety
concerns to be covered by the loft law and that the expanded coverage
would interfere with municipal efforts to attract new manufacturing
enterprises. The amendments in this bill would provide greater
protections to the safety of the tenants of lofts by determining if
their buildings contain unsafe industrial activities. The bill also
exempts units contained in certain industrial zones where such
inclusion could interfere with plans to use these areas for
industrial purposes exclusively. The chapter amendment also contains
increased penalties and enforcement provisions giving the loft board,
the environmental control board and the department of buildings more
authority for ensuring compliance with the law.
This should lead to fewer violations. This bill and the underlying
chapter make the existing loft law permanent. It is the intent of
this legislation to confirm that the law is now permanent; the
temporary extension of the law in the emergency budget extenders did
not indicate a contrary intent.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
New legislation.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None to the state.

EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately; provided, however, sections one, two and three of this
act shall take effect on the same date as a chapter of the laws of
2010, amending the multiple dwelling law relating to interim multiple
dwellings in a city of more than one million persons, as proposed in
legislative bill numbers S.7178-A and A.5667-C, takes effect.
